name: Amedy city
description: Amedy is a historic hilltop city north of Duhok. The Iraqi submission published by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre describes its elevated plateau setting, ancient gates, minaret and other historic remains. The city appears on Iraq's Tentative List, with a submission date of 2 February 2011; this is not World Heritage inscription.

name: Delal Bridge
description: Delal Bridge, also identified as Zakho Bridge in the KRG United States representation's tourism overview, is a historic stone bridge in Zakho. Approved KRG sources identify it as part of the region's architectural heritage. Its construction period is not established in this draft because the captured sources describe its origin with differing levels of certainty.

name: Faida Archaeological Canal and Reliefs
description: The Faida archaeological site includes an irrigation canal with rock-carved reliefs in the southern part of Duhok province, as described by the Kurdistan Regional Government. A Ministry of Municipalities and Tourism report dated 16 October 2022 records the inauguration of the first phase of an archaeological park and attributes the carvings to the Assyrian period.

name: Choli Minaret
description: Choli Minaret is a historic monument in Erbil. An August 2025 KRG report describes its 37-metre tower and planned structural and exterior restoration; that dated plan does not establish whether the work is complete today.

name: Erbil Citadel
description: Erbil Citadel is a fortified settlement built on an archaeological mound in Erbil Governorate. Its urban layout preserves features of the Ottoman period, with historic houses and streets forming a distinctive settlement above the surrounding city. UNESCO inscribed the property on the World Heritage List in 2014.

name: Shanidar Cave
description: Shanidar Cave is an archaeological site in the Zagros Mountains of Erbil Governorate, associated with Neanderthal remains. The KRG tourism overview highlights its importance for studying early human history.

name: Kirkuk Citadel
description: Kirkuk Citadel is a historic elevated settlement in the centre of Kirkuk. The Iraqi submission describes traditional neighbourhoods, entrances and religious buildings. The property appears on Iraq's Tentative List, submitted on 6 April 2021.

name: Mother of Sorrows Church, Kirkuk Citadel
description: The Mother of Sorrows Church is a Chaldean Christian heritage building in Kirkuk Citadel. The Iraqi submission associates it with the Hammam neighbourhood and describes stone-and-plaster construction, arches and marble columns.

name: Prophet Daniel Mosque, Kirkuk Citadel
description: Prophet Daniel Mosque is a religious monument within Kirkuk Citadel. The Iraqi submission describes its brick minaret, arches and courtyard, and records its social and spiritual significance.

name: The Green Dome, Kirkuk Citadel
description: The Green Dome is a decorated octagonal building within Kirkuk Citadel. The Iraqi submission describes its architectural form, coloured tile decoration and inscriptions as part of the citadel's historic fabric.

name: Al-Nouri Mosque and al-Hadba Minaret
description: Al-Nouri Mosque and its al-Hadba minaret are significant Islamic monuments in Mosul's Old City. The Iraqi submission describes the minaret's architectural role and its importance as a symbol of the city.

name: Dominican Church and Clock Tower, Mosul
description: The Dominican Church is a Christian heritage landmark in Mosul. The Iraqi Old City submission identifies its clock tower as a prominent part of the historic skyline alongside the al-Hadba minaret.

name: Hatra
description: Hatra is an ancient fortified city southwest of Mosul associated with the Parthian world. UNESCO describes its circular urban form, defensive walls and temples, whose architecture combines several regional traditions. The property was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1985.

name: Lalish Temple
description: Lalish is a major Yazidi religious complex and pilgrimage centre. The Iraqi submission describes the sacred valley, temple architecture and the tomb of Sheikh Uday bin Musafir. It identifies the site in Sheikhan, Nineveh Governorate, and places it on Iraq's Tentative List with a submission date of 15 April 2020.

name: Nimrud
description: Nimrud, also known as Kalhu, is an Assyrian archaeological city south of Mosul. The Iraqi submission describes defensive walls, raised architectural areas and royal tomb discoveries. The site appears on Iraq's Tentative List, submitted on 7 July 2000; this is not World Heritage inscription.

name: Old City of Mosul
description: Mosul's Old City is a historic urban area on the western bank of the Tigris in Ninewa. The Iraqi submission describes traditional streets, houses, markets and diverse religious buildings. It appears on Iraq's Tentative List, submitted on 17 August 2018.

name: The Ancient City of Nineveh
description: Ancient Nineveh was an important Assyrian political centre on the eastern side of the Tigris at Mosul. The Iraqi submission describes its walls, gateways, mounds and palace remains. It appears on Iraq's Tentative List, submitted on 7 July 2000; this is not World Heritage inscription.

name: Bestansur Neolithic settlement
description: Bestansur is an Early Neolithic archaeological settlement on the edge of the Shahrizor Plain in Sulaymaniyah province. The Iraqi submission published by UNESCO describes mud-brick buildings and evidence of early village life. The site appears on Iraq's Tentative List, with a submission date of 20 January 2017.

name: Qalatga Darband
description: Qalatga Darband is a Hellenistic archaeological city in Sulaymaniyah Governorate. The KRG tourism overview associates its investigation with drone surveys and excavations led by the British Museum.

name: Tell Shemshara
description: Tell Shemshara is an archaeological settlement on the Rania Plain near Lake Dukan. The Kurdistan Regional Government representation in the United States describes it as an early urban settlement and mentions tablet finds associated with the Old Babylonian period.

name: Al-Mustansiriya Madrasa
description: An Abbasid school on the eastern bank of the Tigris in Baghdad, with rooms and iwans arranged around a large central space.

coverImage.alt: Ornamental brick portal at Al-Mustansiriya Madrasa, Baghdad
coverImage.caption: Al-Mustansiriya Madrasa — Wikimedia Commons photograph

name: Abbasid Palace
description: A surviving Abbasid building beside the Tigris in Baghdad, distinguished by its brick-and-lime construction and ornamental brickwork.

coverImage.alt: Decorated entrance of the Abbasid Palace, Baghdad
coverImage.caption: Abbasid Palace — Wikimedia Commons photograph

heritage_status: Component of the Baghdad Rusafa Tigris riverbank ensemble on Iraq's Tentative List; not an individual World Heritage inscription

name: Al-Qishla and Clock Tower
description: A riverside heritage complex in Baghdad, with Ottoman barracks and a clock tower. Its architecture also records later additions during British rule.
heritage_status: Component of the Baghdad Rusafa Tigris riverbank ensemble on Iraq's Tentative List; not an individual World Heritage inscription

name: Al-Wazir Mosque
description: A historic Baghdad mosque associated with the Ottoman governor Hassan Pasha. Its fabric has undergone successive restoration and rebuilding campaigns.

galleryImages.alt: Interior tilework and mihrab of Al-Wazir Mosque, Baghdad
galleryImages.caption: Al-Wazir Mosque — Wikimedia Commons photograph

publication_approval.reviewedBy: Codex (AI evidence and visual review, P6-02 to P6-05)

heritage_status: Component of the Baghdad Rusafa Tigris riverbank ensemble on Iraq's Tentative List; not an individual World Heritage inscription

name: Al-Asifiyah Mosque
description: An Ottoman-era mosque in Baghdad. The Iraqi submission describes a prayer hall with two domes, two minarets and later restoration.
heritage_status: Component of the Baghdad Rusafa Tigris riverbank ensemble on Iraq's Tentative List; not an individual World Heritage inscription

name: House of Wisdom (Industries School Building)
description: An Ottoman-era school building in Baghdad, described as the Industries School or House of Wisdom, with two storeys and arcaded corridors overlooking gardens.
heritage_status: Component of the Baghdad Rusafa Tigris riverbank ensemble on Iraq's Tentative List; not an individual World Heritage inscription

name: Samarra Archaeological City
description: Samarra preserves the plan and monumental remains of an Abbasid capital beside the Tigris. Its mosques, palaces and decorative arts record a major stage in Islamic urban architecture.

name: Great Mosque of Samarra and Malwiya Minaret
description: The ninth-century Great Mosque and its spiral minaret are prominent monuments of Samarra. UNESCO identifies them within the archaeological remains of the Abbasid capital.

coverImage.alt: Malwiya spiral minaret at the Great Mosque of Samarra
coverImage.caption: Great Mosque of Samarra and Malwiya Minaret (photographed in 2021)

license_review.reviewedBy: Codex (AI evidence and visual review, P6-02 to P6-05)

publication_approval.reviewedBy: Codex (AI evidence and visual review, P6-02 to P6-05)

heritage_status: Monument within site-salah-al-din-samarra; no separate UNESCO inscription is asserted.

name: Abu Dulaf Mosque
description: Abu Dulaf is one of the large mosques preserved in Samarra. Its unusual minaret and architectural planning contribute to the Abbasid archaeological city documented by UNESCO.

coverImage.alt: Brick arcades and spiral minaret of Abu Dulaf Mosque, Samarra
coverImage.caption: Abu Dulaf Mosque (photographed in 2001)

publication_approval.reviewedBy: Codex (AI evidence and visual review, P6-02 to P6-05)

heritage_status: Monument within site-salah-al-din-samarra; no separate UNESCO inscription is asserted.

name: Caliphal Palace (Qasr al-Khalifa)
description: The Caliphal Palace, named Qasr al-Khalifa by UNESCO, is one of the palace remains within Samarra. It belongs to the monumental landscape of the former Abbasid capital.
heritage_status: Monument within site-salah-al-din-samarra; no separate UNESCO inscription is asserted.

name: Ashur (Qal'at Sherqat)
description: Ashur is an ancient city beside the Tigris with temples, palaces and royal burials. It was an Assyrian political and religious centre and later revived under Parthian rule.

name: Qaysari Bazaar, Erbil
description: Qaysari Bazaar is a historic market in downtown Erbil. A May 2024 KRG report documents a fire and describes collaborative restoration efforts with UNESCO; it does not establish the market's current condition.

name: Red Terror Museum, Slemani
description: The Red Terror Museum in Slemani interprets repression under Ba'athist rule. The KRG's regional tourism overview identifies it as a place for learning about the region's modern history.

name: Al-Qaysariyah Market, Kirkuk
description: Al-Qaysariyah Market stands on the eastern side of Kirkuk Citadel. Iraq's UNESCO submission describes its commercial rooms, shops and arched upper-storey architecture.
heritage_status: Monument within site-kirkuk-kirkuk-citadel; no separate UNESCO inscription is asserted.

name: Great Mosque of Erbil Citadel
description: The Great (Mulla Afandi) Mosque is the only religious building still standing on Erbil Citadel. Its founding date is unknown; the mosque is recorded on the citadel from the 13th century, and its present single-domed roof dates from a 1959 reconstruction. A 2025 KRG release lists its restoration among recent citadel works.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Regional Government, August 2025 citadel restoration release

review_notes: Wikidata gives inception 1797; the citadel sources say the founding date is unknown. Period left empty.

name: Erbil Citadel Hammam
description: The hammam is the oldest bathhouse on Erbil Citadel and is dated to the 18th century (1775 in the UNESCO documentation). A January 2025 KRG release reported its US-funded restoration as nearly finished.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments catalogue
Kurdistan Regional Government, January 2025 citadel renovation release

review_notes: UNESCO date 1775 reported via search snippet; confirm against the nomination file.

name: House B13 (37 Topkhana)
description: A historic courtyard house in the Topkhana quarter of Erbil Citadel, documented in Columbia University’s Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments survey.

sources.sourceName: Columbia University, Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments catalogue
Columbia MCID — House B13 image record

name: Rashid Agha House
description: A historic house in Erbil documented in Columbia University’s Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments catalogue.

description: A historic house in Erbil documented in Columbia University’s Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments catalogue.

description: A historic house in Erbil documented in Columbia University’s Mapping Mesopotamian Monuments catalogue.

name: Kurdish Textile and Cultural Museum
description: A museum of Kurdish textiles and crafts founded in 2004 in a renovated mansion in the south-east quarter of Erbil Citadel. It also works to keep traditional weaving methods alive.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Kurdish Textile and Cultural Museum

name: Erbil Civilization Museum
description: Erbil’s archaeological museum, the second largest in the Kurdistan Region, with finds from prehistory to the late Abbasid period. The museum began in the 1960s, moved into the citadel in the 1970s and later to its own building.

name: Khalidiya Khanqah Mosque and Tekke
description: A Naqshbandi Sufi complex of mosque, tekke, library and market beside Erbil Citadel. It was founded in 1805 by Mullah Hidayatullah al-Arbili at the request of Mawlana Khalid al-Naqshbandi and rebuilt in 1961. The surrounding Khanqah quarter takes its name from it.

sources.sourceName: Wikipedia — Khalidiya Khanqah Mosque and Tekke

name: Mausoleum of Sultan Muzaffar
description: A mausoleum attributed to Sultan Muzaffar al-Din Gökböri, the 12th–13th-century ruler of Erbil, near the Erbil Governorate building. It is one of several historic tombs in the old bazaar area.
review_notes: Single opinion-article source; attribution and fabric date need verification.

name: Grave of Prophet Uzair (Ezra), Erbil
description: A grave venerated as that of the Prophet Uzair (Ezra), near the Sheikh Choli Mosque in Erbil’s old bazaar district.
review_notes: Traditional attribution reported by one opinion article; not a historical identification.

name: Jewish Cemetery of Erbil
description: Erbil’s historic Jewish cemetery, a reminder of the city’s former Jewish community.
review_notes: Exact location not given by the source.

name: St. George’s Church, Ankawa
description: Mar Gewargis is described as the oldest Chaldean Catholic church in Ankawa. The building is probably from the 9th century, with parts possibly older, and was restored in 1995.
review_notes: Wikipedia article flagged as needing citations; treat the 816 date as unverified.

name: Mart Shmoni Church, Ankawa
description: A Syriac Catholic church dedicated to Mart Shmoni in Ankawa, the Christian suburb of Erbil.
review_notes: No construction date found; heritage significance needs a documented source.

name: Melqi (Mar Qardagh tradition), Ankawa
description: Ankawa has been linked to the Neo-Assyrian town of Milqia, seat of an Akitu house of Ishtar near Arbela. Melqi is the martyrdom and burial place of Saint Mar Qardagh in the Syriac History of Mar Qardagh, and the saint is still venerated in Ankawa.
review_notes: Scholarly identification (Parpola) and hagiographic tradition, not an excavated site.

name: Qasr Shemamok (Kilizu)
description: A 20-hectare tell rising about 30 m above the plain, 30 km south of Erbil on the Shiwazor river, with a lower town of about 50 hectares. Under the Assyrians it was Kilizu, a provincial capital; remains run from Hurrian and Assyrian to Parthian and Sasanian times. A French mission has excavated there since 2011.

sources.sourceName: Encyclopaedia Iranica — Kilizu i. The site
Ur et al., The Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey: Preliminary Results, 2012–2020 (IRAQ 83, 2021)

name: Kurd Qaburstan
description: A large walled city 22 km south-west of Erbil, mainly of the Middle Bronze Age (early 2nd millennium BC) and proposed as ancient Qabra. A UCF-led team found evidence of a siege in 2025, together with the first substantial group of cuneiform tablets from the Erbil region.

sources.sourceName: University of Central Florida news — excavation at Kurd Qaburstan
Kurdistan24, 13 July 2025 — Excavations conclude at ancient sites in southwestern Erbil
Ur et al., The Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey: Preliminary Results, 2012–2020 (IRAQ 83, 2021)

approximateLocation: Next to Yedi Kizlar village, Shamamok sub-district
review_notes: Kurdistan24 reports the excavation under the village name Yadi Qzlar; Wikipedia places Yedi Kizlar on the lower town, so they are treated as one site.

name: Tell Baqrta
description: A major mound near Qasr Shemamok that reached about 80 hectares in the Early Bronze Age. It was recorded by the Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey.

sources.sourceName: Ur et al., The Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey: Preliminary Results, 2012–2020 (IRAQ 83, 2021)

name: Gird-i Matrab
description: A tell about 30 km south of Erbil, first identified by the Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey in 2012. Excavations by Bryn Mawr College since 2022 found Late Chalcolithic levels from the 5th millennium BC, an Iron Age reoccupation and a Hellenistic quarter; under the Seleucids and Parthians it grew to about 25 hectares.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan24, 26 July 2025 — Vast multi-era settlement uncovered near Erbil
Kurdistan24, 22 October 2026 — Gird-i Matrab excavation renewed
Ur et al., The Erbil Plain Archaeological Survey: Preliminary Results, 2012–2020 (IRAQ 83, 2021)

name: Gird Lashkir
description: A tell with about 14 m of deposits over some 4 hectares near Wadi Kasnazan, close to Kasnazan and Banaslawa. Excavations by the Autonomous University of Barcelona since 2015 found Halaf and Ubaid levels and occupation into the 1st millennium BC; reports describe it as a trade centre in 3500–2000 BC.

sources.sourceName: Popular Archaeology — Iraqi Kurdistan site reveals evolution toward the first cities of Mesopotamia
SyriacPress, 13 June 2024 — Spanish team unearths Bronze Age city in Erbil

approximateLocation: Near Wadi Kasnazan, east of Erbil

name: Sheikh Ahmad archaeological site
description: An excavated archaeological site on the Erbil–Koya road, shown in a 2026 Rudaw report on Erbil’s archaeology. The Wikipedia list of Erbil sites names it Girdi Sheikh Ahmed.

description: A tell south-west of Erbil listed among the governorate’s archaeological sites.

name: Satu Qala (Idu)
description: A tell on the right bank of the Lower Zab, 70 km south-east of Erbil, identified as ancient Idu. It was a Middle Assyrian provincial capital, then the seat of independent kings, and stayed occupied into the Middle Islamic period.

name: Khanzad Castle
description: A two-storey stone and gypsum castle on a hilltop 22 km from Erbil on the Erbil–Shaqlawa road. It was built in the late 16th century by Mir Khanzad, ruler of the Soran Emirate, as her residence and to defend Erbil.

sources.sourceName: Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

name: Dwin Castle
description: A castle in the mountain village of Dwin, about 31 km north-east of Erbil, long linked by local tradition to the family of Saladin. Research began in 2014 with Pázmány Péter Catholic University and Salahaddin University; restoration plans were reviewed in 2025.

sources.sourceName: Shafaq News — Dwin Castle restoration revives Ayyubid link
Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

review_notes: The Saladin birthplace link is local tradition, not documented fact.

name: Rabban Boya Shrine
description: A cave shrine at about 1,070 m above Shaqlawa, sacred since early Christian times and shared by Christians and Muslims, who know it as Sheikh Wso Rahman. It was recognised as a historic site in 1945; an old church and cemetery lie nearby.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Chronicle — Raban Boya: One Shrine, Two Faiths
Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

name: Batas-Harir Rock Relief
description: A rock relief of a standing figure carved on the cliff of Mount Harir above the villages of Batas and Harir. Its date is debated: the dress suggests the Parthian period, and one reading identifies the figure as a ruler of Adiabene of the 1st century AD.

sources.sourceName: World History Encyclopedia — Rock relief of Mountain Hareer

review_notes: Pin is on Harir town (Wikidata), not the relief itself. See Grabowski 2011 for the scholarly study.

name: Dere Castle
description: A ruined castle about 40 km north of Erbil on the Erbil–Rawanduz road. Sources disagree on its age: some attribute it to Muhammad Pasha of Soran in the 19th century, others to an older foundation that was rebuilt.

sources.sourceName: Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

name: Rawanduz Old Town
description: The old quarters of Rawanduz keep narrow lanes and flat-roofed stone houses. Rawanduz was founded by the Rawadid dynasty in the 10th century and was capital of the Soran Emirate until 1836. In 2023 the government began buying and restoring historic houses, starting with ten.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 2023 — Government initiates process to preserve Rawanduz historic houses

name: Qalat Lokhan
description: A fortification on the northern edge of Rawanduz, discussed with the other late-Islamic castles of the Soran region.

sources.sourceName: Annali di Ca' Foscari. Serie orientale 60 (2024)

name: Gird-i Dasht
description: The largest known mound in the Soran area, rising about 20 m above the plain. The Rowanduz Archaeological Program excavated and surveyed it from 2013.

sources.sourceName: Academia.edu — Rowanduz Archaeological Program first report
Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

name: Gund-i Topzawa
description: A burned early Iron Age settlement near Sidakan, cut into a hillside and uncovered when road widening in 2013 disturbed it. Radiocarbon dates place its construction in the early 1st millennium BC, and its destruction fits Sargon II’s campaign against Musasir in 714 BC.

sources.sourceName: Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

name: Topzawa Stele
description: A bilingual Urartian–Assyrian stele near Sidakan recording a campaign to Musasir by the Urartian king Rusa I. Sources disagree whether it is still in place or held in Erbil.
review_notes: Current custody disputed (in situ vs. Erbil museum). Year is the approximate reign of Rusa I.

name: Kelashin Stele
description: A stele at the Kelashin pass bearing an Urartian–Akkadian bilingual text of about 800 BC, first described in 1827. It records the Urartian king Ishpuini taking the city of Musasir (Ardini).
review_notes: The stele sits on the Iraq–Iran border; sources disagree on its present custody.

name: Mudjesir (proposed Musasir temple of Haldi)
description: Column bases and statues found in the village of Mudjesir have been linked to the temple of Haldi at Musasir (Ardini), sacked by Sargon II in 714 BC. The identification is a working hypothesis; other candidates lie in Iran.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 22 July 2014 — A stunning find in Kurdistan
Penn Museum, Expedition 56(3) — Searching for the Kingdom of Musasir

name: Bestoon Cave
description: A cave in the Bradost mountains south-west of Soran where 1950s work with Fuad Safar found Neolithic remains. It has been developed for visitors.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

name: Diyan Cave
description: A cave on Bradost mountain near Hawdiyan, listed with Bestoon Cave among the heritage destinations of Erbil Governorate.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Regional Government, Board of Investment — Doing Business in the Kurdistan Region

name: Zawi Chemi Shanidar
description: An open-air settlement below Shanidar Cave excavated by Ralph Solecki, important for the transition to settled life in the Zagros.

sources.sourceName: PLOS ONE — The Zagros Epipalaeolithic revisited (Palegawra)

name: Plngan Cave
description: A cave at the foot of Plngan Mountain in Soran where the Soran antiquities department and the Autonomous University of Barcelona reported human footprints and remains of the late Old and early Middle Stone Age in 2025.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 17 May 2025 — Stone Age footprints discovered in Soran

name: Bana Helk
description: A hilltop Neolithic village north of Erbil where Kurdish and Spanish archaeologists found Halaf-period remains and decorated pottery.

sources.sourceName: Rudaw, 29 May 2022 — Traces of Halaf culture discovered in north Erbil

name: Mar Gewargis Church, Bedyal
description: The historic church of Bedyal, one of the oldest Christian villages of the Barzan area. In 2025 the Assyrian Church of the East patriarch called for careful restoration of the region’s historic churches.

sources.sourceName: Kurdistan Chronicle — A Christian village in the heart of Kurdistan’s mountains
SyriacPress, 12 August 2025 — Patriarch Mar Awa III on historic churches

name: Old Town of Koya
description: The late-Ottoman old town of Koya (Koy Sanjaq), with architecture rarely found elsewhere in the Kurdistan Region. ALIPH and WADI have funded emergency stabilisation and documentation. The Bayz Agha and Hawawan quarters are among its oldest.

sources.sourceName: ALIPH Foundation — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya
WADI — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya

name: Grand Mosque of Koya
description: One of Koya’s oldest landmarks, founded in 1844, with a domed ceiling carrying Qur’anic inscriptions, marble columns and a stone minbar. An archaeological field study was published by Zeidan Rashid in 2013.

sources.sourceName: Annals of the Faculty of Arts, Ain Shams University — Zeidan Rashid, The Great Mosque of Koysinjaq

name: Haji Bakr Agha Qaysari, Koya
description: A covered market of more than 90 shops built in 1840, described as one of the oldest bazaars in Iraqi Kurdistan and still in use.

sources.sourceName: World Monuments Fund on Google Arts & Culture — Qaisari Bazaar in Koya

name: Mahmud Agha Khan, Koya
description: A two-storey stone, gypsum and timber caravanserai of 1861–62 with 64 rooms at the centre of Koya’s bazaar, one of the town’s four old khans. WADI stabilised its endangered structures; Kurdistan24 described it as neglected in 2025.

sources.sourceName: WADI — Safeguarding the Old Town of Koya

name: Mulla Abdul Majid House, Koya
description: A two-storey mud, lime and timber house with two courtyards and a hexagonal fountain, restored as a heritage museum of life about 250 years ago.

name: Mulla Kura House, Koya
description: Described as one of the most prominent historic houses of Koya.

name: Mar Bena Church, Armota
description: A church at Armota near Koya linked to the Monastery of Mar Behnam, said to date from the 4th century. It was destroyed in 1988 and rebuilt in 1996.

name: Mart Mariam Church, Armota
description: The village church of Armota, built in 1868 and renovated in 1979 and 2009. The village also has a church of Mar Michael and a shrine of Mart Shmune.
